questions.explaination: With binary semaphore $s=1$ (I-1), mutual exclusion guarantees serialized critical section access, yielding net change $+5 - 3 = +2 \implies V_1 = 10 + 2 = 12$. With counting semaphore $s=2$ (I-2), two threads can enter simultaneously; a decrement thread can read $X=10$, be preempted while all 5 increments and 2 decrements complete, and then write back $10-1 = 9$, repeatedly clobbering increments to achieve minimum $V_2 = 10 - 3 = 7$.

Consider the context-free grammar G below
S
→
aSb | X
X
→
aX | Xb | a | b ,
where S and X are non-terminals, and a and b are terminal symbols. The starting
non-terminal is S.
Which one of the following statements is CORRECT?

options.A: The language generated by G is (a + b)∗
options.B: The language generated by G is a∗(a + b)b∗
options.C: The language generated by G is a∗b∗(a + b)
options.D:
The language generated by G is not a regular language
CS

questions.explaination: The subgrammar $X \to aX \mid Xb \mid a \mid b$ derives all non-empty strings with any number of $a$'s followed by any number of $b$'s having at least one $a$ or $b$, described by $a^*(a+b)b^*$. Rule $S \to aSb \mid X$ prefixes $k$ $a$'s and suffixes $k$ $b$'s ($k \ge 0$), yielding $a^k a^*(a+b)b^* b^k = a^*(a+b)b^*$. Because this language is represented by a regular expression, it is a regular language.

Consider the given C-code and its corresponding assembly code, with a few
operands U1–U4 being unknown. Some useful information as well as the semantics
of each unique assembly instruction is annotated as inline comments in the code.
The memory is byte-addressable.
//C-code
int a[10], b[10], i;
// int is 32-bit
for (i=0; i<10;i++)
a[i] = b[i] * 8;
;assembly-code (; indicates comments)
;r1-r5 are 32-bit integer registers
;initialize r1=0, r2=10
;initialize r3, r4 with base address of a, b
L01: jeq r1, r2, end
;if(r1==r2) goto end
L02: lw
r5, 0(r4)
;r5 <- Memory[r4+0]
L03: shl r5, r5, U1
;r5 <- r5 << U1
L04: sw
r5, 0(r3)
;Memory[r3+0] <- r5
L05: add r3, r3, U2
;r3 <- r3+U2
L06: add r4, r4, U3
L07: add r1, r1, 1
L08: jmp U4
;goto U4
L09: end
Which one of the following options is a CORRECT replacement for operands in
the position (U1, U2, U3, U4) in the above assembly code?
questions.explaination: Multiplying by 8 corresponds to shifting left by 3 bits ($2^3 = 8$), so $U_1 = 3$. Since elements are 32-bit (4-byte) integers in byte-addressable memory, the pointers in registers `r3` and `r4` must advance by 4 bytes each iteration, so $U_2 = 4$ and $U_3 = 4$. Finally, the loop branches back to the condition check at label $L_{01}$, so $U_4 = L_{01}$.

Consider the IEEE-754 single precision ﬂoating point numbers
P=0xC1800000 and Q=0x3F5C2EF4.
Which one of the following corresponds to the product of these numbers
(i.e., P × Q), represented in the IEEE-754 single precision format?
questions.subtopic: Number representations and computer arithmetic (fixed and floating point)
questions.explaination: Number $P = \text{0xC1800000}$ has sign bit 1, biased exponent $131$, actual exponent $131 - 127 = 4$, and mantissa $1.0$, so $P = -16.0 = -2^4$. Number $Q = \text{0x3F5C2EF4}$ is positive with biased exponent $126$ (exponent $-1$) and mantissa fraction `5C2EF4`. Multiplying $P \times Q$ flips the sign to negative (1), adds 4 to the exponent (biased exponent becomes $126 + 4 = 130 = \text{0x82}$), and retains the mantissa fraction, resulting in `0xC15C2EF4`.

questions.question_text:
Let A be a priority queue for maintaining a set of elements.
Suppose A is
implemented using a max-heap data structure. The operation Extract-Max(A)
extracts and deletes the maximum element from A. The operation Insert(A,key)
inserts a new element key in A. The properties of a max-heap are preserved at the
end of each of these operations.
When A contains n elements, which one of the following statements about the worst
case running time of these two operations is TRUE?

options.A: Both Extract-Max(A) and Insert(A,key) run in O(1).
options.B: Both Extract-Max(A) and Insert(A,key) run in O(log(n)).
options.C: Extract-Max(A) runs in O(1) whereas Insert(A,key) runs in O(n).
options.D:
Extract-Max(A) runs in O(1) whereas Insert(A,key) runs in O(log(n)).
CS

questions.subtopic: Trees, binary search trees, binary heaps
questions.explaination: In a binary max-heap of $n$ elements, `Extract-Max` replaces the root with the last element and performs `maxHeapify` downward along the height $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$, running in $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ worst-case time. `Insert` places the new key at the next leaf position and sifts upward along the height, also running in $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ worst-case time.

The properties of a max-heap are preserved at the end of each of these operations.

options_latex.D: `Extract-Max(A)` runs in $\mathcal{O}(1)$ whereas `Insert(A,key)` runs in $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$.

questions.question_text:
Let U = {1, 2, . . . , n}, where n is a large positive integer greater than 1000. Let
k be a positive integer less than n. Let A, B be subsets of U with |A| = |B| = k
and A ∩B = ∅. We say that a permutation of U separates A from B if one of the
following is true.
- All members of A appear in the permutation before any of the members of B.
- All members of B appear in the permutation before any of the members of A.
How many permutations of U separate A from B?
questions.subtopic: Combinatorics: counting, recurrence relations, generating functions
questions.explaination: There are 2 orderings for which block appears first ($A$ before $B$ or $B$ before $A$). There are $\binom{n}{2k}$ ways to choose the positions in the permutation for elements of $A \cup B$. The first $k$ chosen positions must contain elements of the first set ($k!$ permutations) and the next $k$ positions contain elements of the second set ($k!$ permutations). The remaining $n - 2k$ elements can be arranged in any of the $(n - 2k)!$ remaining positions. Total valid permutations $= 2 \binom{n}{2k} (n - 2k)! (k!)^2$.

Let f : A →B be an onto (or surjective) function, where A and B are nonempty
sets. Deﬁne an equivalence relation ∼on the set A as
a1 ∼a2 if f(a1) = f(a2) ,
where a1, a2 ∈A. Let E = {[x] : x ∈A} be the set of all the equivalence classes
under ∼. Deﬁne a new mapping F : E →B as
F([x]) = f(x),
for all the equivalence classes [x] in E.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.B: F is an onto (or surjective) function.
options.C: F is a one-to-one (or injective) function.
options.D:
F is a bijective function.
CS

questions.subtopic: Sets, relations, functions, partial orders and lattices
questions.explaination: By the fundamental theorem of equivalence relations and canonical function decomposition, $F([x]) = f(x)$ is well-defined and injective because $[x_1] = [x_2] \iff f(x_1) = f(x_2)$ (C is TRUE). Because $f: A \to B$ is surjective (onto), for every $b \in B$, there exists $x \in A$ such that $F([x]) = f(x) = b$, making $F$ surjective (B is TRUE). Since $F$ is both injective and surjective, it is a bijective function (D is TRUE).

questions.question_text:
Suppose you are asked to design a new reliable byte-stream transport protocol
like TCP. This protocol, named myTCP, runs over a 100 Mbps network with Round
Trip Time of 150 milliseconds and the maximum segment lifetime of 2 minutes.
Which of the following is/are valid lengths of the Sequence Number ﬁeld in the
myTCP header?
questions.subtopic: Transport layer: flow control and congestion control, UDP, TCP, sockets
questions.explaination: To prevent sequence number wraparound within the Maximum Segment Lifetime ($MSL = 2\text{ min} = 120\text{ s}$), the sequence number space $2^k$ must be at least the data bytes transmitted at line rate during MSL: $2^k \ge \frac{100 \times 10^6\text{ bps}}{8} \times 120\text{ s} = 1.5 \times 10^9\text{ bytes}$. Since $2^{30} \approx 1.07 \times 10^9 < 1.5 \times 10^9$ and $2^{31} \approx 2.15 \times 10^9 > 1.5 \times 10^9$, at least 31 bits are required. Thus, 32 bits, 34 bits, and 36 bits are all valid lengths.

questions.question_text:
Let X be a set and 2X denote the powerset of X.
Deﬁne a binary operation Δ on 2X as follows:
AΔB = (A −B) ∪(B −A) .
Let H = (2X, Δ). Which of the following statements about H is/are correct?

options.B: Every element in H has an inverse, but H is NOT a group.
options.C: For every A ∈2X, the inverse of A is the complement of A.
options.D:
For every A ∈2X, the inverse of A is A.
CS

questions.explaination: Symmetric difference $\Delta$ is associative on $2^X$. The identity element is the empty set $\emptyset$, since $A \Delta \emptyset = A$. Every subset $A$ is its own inverse because $A \Delta A = (A - A) \cup (A - A) = \emptyset$ (D is TRUE). Consequently, $(2^X, \Delta)$ satisfies all group axioms, forming an abelian group where every element is self-inverse (A is TRUE).

questions.question_text:
Suppose in a web browser, you click on the www.gate-2023.in URL. The browser
cache is empty. The IP address for this URL is not cached in your local host, so
a DNS lookup is triggered (by the local DNS server deployed on your local host)
over the 3-tier DNS hierarchy in an iterative mode. No resource records are cached
anywhere across all DNS servers.
Let RTT denote the round trip time between your local host and DNS servers
in the DNS hierarchy. The round trip time between the local host and the web
server hosting www.gate-2023.in is also equal to RTT. The HTML ﬁle associated
with the URL is small enough to have negligible transmission time and negligible
rendering time by your web browser, which references 10 equally small objects on
the same web server.
Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT about the minimum elapsed
time between clicking on the URL and your browser fully rendering it?

options.A: 7 RTTs, in case of non-persistent HTTP with 5 parallel TCP connections.
options.B: 5 RTTs, in case of persistent HTTP with pipelining.
options.C: 9 RTTs, in case of non-persistent HTTP with 5 parallel TCP connections.
options.D:
6 RTTs, in case of persistent HTTP with pipelining.
CS

questions.subtopic: Application layer protocols: DNS, SMTP, HTTP, FTP, Email
questions.explaination: Resolving the URL via 3-tier iterative DNS requires $3\text{ RTT}$. Initiating TCP connection and requesting the base HTML page requires $1 + 1 = 2\text{ RTT}$, so the base HTML is received after $3 + 2 = 5\text{ RTT}$. With persistent HTTP pipelining, all 10 objects are fetched in 1 round trip over the established connection, giving $5 + 1 = 6\text{ RTT}$ (D is TRUE). With non-persistent HTTP and 5 parallel connections, fetching 10 objects takes 2 sequential batches; each batch takes $1\text{ RTT (TCP)} + 1\text{ RTT (HTTP)} = 2\text{ RTT}$, adding $2 \times 2 = 4\text{ RTT}$, giving $5 + 4 = 9\text{ RTT}$ (C is TRUE).

questions.question_text:
Consider a random experiment where two fair coins are tossed. Let A be the event
that denotes HEAD on both the throws, B be the event that denotes HEAD on
the ﬁrst throw, and C be the event that denotes HEAD on the second throw.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.explaination: Sample space $S = \{HH, HT, TH, TT\}$. Events are $A = \{HH\}$, $B = \{HH, HT\}$, $C = \{HH, TH\}$. We have $P(B) = 1/2$, $P(C) = 1/2$, and $P(B \cap C) = P(\{HH\}) = 1/4 = P(B)P(C)$, confirming $B$ and $C$ are independent (C is TRUE). By independence, $\text{Prob}(B|C) = \text{Prob}(B)$ (D is TRUE). $P(A \cap B) = 1/4 \neq P(A)P(B) = 1/8$, so $A$ and $B$ are dependent.

questions.question_text:
Consider functions Function 1 and Function 2 expressed in pseudocode as
follows:
Function 1
while n > 1 do
for i = 1 to n do
x = x + 1;
end for
n = ⌊n/2⌋;
end while
Function 2
for i = 1 to 100 ∗n do
x = x + 1;
end for
Let f1(n) and f2(n) denote the number of times the statement “x = x + 1” is
executed in Function 1 and Function 2, respectively.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.subtopic: Asymptotic worst case time and space complexity
questions.explaination: In Function 1, the inner loop executes $n + \lfloor n/2 \rfloor + \lfloor n/4 \rfloor + \dots \approx 2n$ times, which gives $f_1(n) = \Theta(n)$. In Function 2, the loop runs $100n$ times, which gives $f_2(n) = \Theta(n)$. Because both functions have exact linear asymptotic growth, $f_1(n) \in \Theta(f_2(n))$ (A is TRUE) and $f_1(n) \in \mathcal{O}(n)$ (D is TRUE).

questions.question_text:
Let G be a simple, ﬁnite, undirected graph with vertex set {v1, . . . , vn}. Let Δ(G)
denote the maximum degree of G and let N = {1, 2, . . .} denote the set of all possible
colors. Color the vertices of G using the following greedy strategy:
for i = 1, . . . , n
color(vi) ←min{j ∈N :
no neighbour of vi is colored j}
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.A: This procedure results in a proper vertex coloring of G.
options.B: The number of colors used is at most Δ(G) + 1.
options.C: The number of colors used is at most Δ(G).
options.D:
The number of colors used is equal to the chromatic number of G.
CS

questions.explaination: The greedy coloring strategy assigns to each vertex the lowest index color not used by any already-colored neighbor, guaranteeing that adjacent vertices receive distinct colors (proper coloring, so A is TRUE). Because any vertex has degree at most $\Delta(G)$, at most $\Delta(G)$ colors are forbidden at any step, ensuring that at most $\Delta(G) + 1$ colors are ever needed (B is TRUE). Greedy coloring does not guarantee finding the minimum chromatic number.

options_latex.A: This procedure results in a proper vertex coloring of $G$.
options_latex.B: The number of colors used is at most $\Delta(G) + 1$.
options_latex.C: The number of colors used is at most $\Delta(G)$.
options_latex.D: The number of colors used is equal to the chromatic number of $G$.

Let U = {1, 2, 3}. Let 2U denote the powerset of U. Consider an undirected graph
G whose vertex set is 2U. For any A, B ∈2U, (A, B) is an edge in G if and only
if (i) A̸ = B, and (ii) either A ⊊B or B ⊊A. For any vertex A in G, the set of
all possible orderings in which the vertices of G can be visited in a Breadth First
Search (BFS) starting from A is denoted by B(A).
If ∅denotes the empty set, then the cardinality of B(∅) is
.

questions.subtopic: Graph traversals, minimum spanning trees, shortest paths
questions.explaination: The vertex set has $2^3 = 8$ vertices. An edge connects $A$ and $B$ iff $A \subsetneq B$ or $B \subsetneq A$. For the empty set $\emptyset$, every non-empty subset $S \subseteq U$ satisfies $\emptyset \subsetneq S$, meaning all 7 non-empty subsets are direct neighbors of $\emptyset$ at BFS depth 1. A BFS starting at $\emptyset$ must visit $\emptyset$ first, and can then visit the 7 distance-1 neighbors in any of the $7! = 5040$ possible orderings.

questions.explaination: Array $D[128][128]$ has 16384 elements stored in row-major order. Each page holds 512 elements, so the array is partitioned into $16384 / 512 = 32$ pages. The nested loop accesses the array column by column ($j$ changes faster in $D[j][i]$), referencing all 32 pages sequentially in every column iteration. Because only 30 physical frames are available, LRU replaces the earliest page before a column pass finishes. Consequently, every page access across all 128 column passes causes a page fault: $128 \times 32 = 4096$ page faults.

questions.question_text:
Consider a computer system with 57-bit virtual addressing using multi-level
tree-structured page tables with L levels for virtual to physical address translation.
The page size is 4 KB (1 KB = 1024 B) and a page table entry at any of the levels
occupies 8 bytes.
The value of L is
.
CS
questions.explaination: Page size is $4\text{ KB} = 2^{12}\text{ bytes}$, which leaves $57 - 12 = 45\text{ bits}$ for the page table hierarchy. Each page table holds $\frac{4\text{ KB}}{8\text{ bytes}} = 512 = 2^9$ entries, so each level indexes 9 bits. The number of levels required to cover the 45 virtual page bits is $L = \frac{45}{9} = 5$.

questions.question_text:
Consider a sequence a of elements a0 = 1, a1 = 5, a2 = 7, a3 = 8, a4 = 9, and
a5 = 2. The following operations are performed on a stack S and a queue Q, both
of which are initially empty.
I: push the elements of a from a0 to a5 in that order into S.
II: enqueue the elements of a from a0 to a5 in that order into Q.
III: pop an element from S.
IV: dequeue an element from Q.
V: pop an element from S.
VI: dequeue an element from Q.
VII: dequeue an element from Q and push the same element into S.
VIII: Repeat operation VII three times.
IX: pop an element from S.
X: pop an element from S.
The top element of S after executing the above operations is
.
CS
questions.explaination: Operations trace: Push $[1, 5, 7, 8, 9, 2]$ to $S$ (top=2); enqueue $[1, 5, 7, 8, 9, 2]$ to $Q$ (front=1). Pop 2 from $S$ ($S=[1,5,7,8,9]$), dequeue 1 from $Q$ ($Q=[5,7,8,9,2]$); pop 9 from $S$ ($S=[1,5,7,8]$), dequeue 5 from $Q$ ($Q=[7,8,9,2]$). Repeating dequeue from $Q$ and push to $S$ 4 times moves $7, 8, 9, 2$ into $S$, making $S=[1,5,7,8,7,8,9,2]$. Finally, two pops remove 2 and 9, leaving 8 at the top of $S$.

\begin{align*}

I &\to I_1 B & I.val &= (2 \cdot I_1.val) + B.val \\

F &\to B F_1 & F.val &= \frac{1}{2}(B.val + F_1.val) \\
F &\to B & F.val &= \frac{1}{2}B.val \\
B &\to 0 & B.val &= 0.val \\
B &\to 1 & B.val &= 1.val
\end{align*}

Consider the language L over the alphabet {0, 1}, given below:
L = {w ∈{0, 1}∗| w does not contain three or more consecutive 1’s}.
The minimum number of states in a Deterministic Finite-State Automaton (DFA)
for L is
.
CS
questions.explaination: The language contains all binary strings not containing `111`. The minimal DFA tracks consecutive 1s: state $q_0$ (0 consecutive 1s, start), state $q_1$ (1 consecutive 1), state $q_2$ (2 consecutive 1s), and state $q_3$ (trap state reached on 3rd consecutive 1). States $q_0, q_1, q_2$ are accepting states. Thus, exactly 4 states are required.

questions.question_text:
An 8-way set associative cache of size 64 KB (1 KB = 1024 bytes) is used in a
system with 32-bit address. The address is sub-divided into TAG, INDEX, and
BLOCK OFFSET.
The number of bits in the TAG is
.
CS
questions.subtopic: Memory hierarchy: cache, main memory and secondary storage
questions.explaination: Address size $= 32\text{ bits}$. Cache size $= 64\text{ KB} = 2^{16}\text{ bytes}$. For an 8-way set-associative cache, the combined capacity of index and offset is $\frac{\text{Cache Size}}{\text{Associativity}} = \frac{64\text{ KB}}{8} = 8\text{ KB} = 2^{13}\text{ bytes}$, requiring $13\text{ bits}$ for INDEX + BLOCK OFFSET. Therefore, the number of TAG bits is $32 - 13 = 19\text{ bits}$.
